# Week 7, Day 5.1 - Prerequisites check

Today you move code out of a spec and into a module. That is `export` / `import`, which you have
used - plus one Playwright type.

| In play | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `export` / `import` (named) | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| `type` aliases for objects | [day1_2](/learn/w7/d1/p2) |
| Typed parameters and return types | [day1_2](/learn/w7/d1/p2) |
| Arrays of objects | [week3/day5_1](/learn/w3/d5/p1) |
| Importing a JSON file | [week5/day5_1](/learn/w5/d5/p1) |

**Next:** [Day 5.2 - Write it once](/learn/w7/d5/p2)

## Returning two things

A helper that creates a user has two useful results: the id and the token. A function returns one
value - so return an **object**, and name the shape.

```ts
export type Account = { userName: string; password: string; userId: string; token: string };

export async function createAccount(...): Promise<Account> { ... }
```

| Alternative | Why not |
|---|---|
| Return an array `[id, token]` | the caller has to remember the order |
| Two functions | two round trips for one job |
| **An object with a named type** | self-documenting, and destructurable |

## Pass `request` in; never import it

This is the rule that surprises people. `request` belongs to the **running test** - Playwright
creates it per test and tears it down after. A module cannot reach for one.

| Written | Result |
|---|---|
| `import { request } from "@playwright/test"` | not a value you can use like that |
| `createAccount(request, ...)` as the first parameter | correct |

Every Playwright helper that touches the network takes it as a parameter. Same reason a page
object takes `page` in its constructor ([week5/day3_2](/learn/w5/d3/p2)).

# Week 7, Day 5.2 - Write it once

Day 4's `beforeAll` was nine lines. Every API spec you write from here needs the same nine. Today
they become one line, and then five near-identical negative tests become one loop.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## The helper module

Not named `.spec.ts` - it calls no `test()`, so the runner never collects it. Same rule as a page
object ([week3/day3_2](/learn/w3/d3/p2)).

| Export | Job |
|---|---|
| `BASE_URL` | one host, one place |
| `type Account` | the shape three files agree on |
| `createAccount(request, prefix)` | create **and** authorise, returning both values |
| `authHeader(account)` | the one repeated header |
| `deleteAccount(request, account)` | tidy up |

Two details worth stopping on:

- **`request` is the first parameter**, per [day5_1](/learn/w7/d5/p1).
- **There are `expect`s inside the helper.** Allowed here because they check the *helper's own
  contract*: if the user was not created, no test using it can mean anything. It is not a test's
  assertion - the same distinction as [week6/day2_2](/learn/w6/d2/p2).

## Five scenarios, one test

The session sets this as homework: registration has a valid case and several invalid ones, and
writing five near-identical tests is the wrong answer.

Put the differences in **data**:

| Case | Status | Code | Message |
|---|---|---|---|
| valid | **201** | - | - |
| password too weak | **400** | 1300 | `Passwords must have at least...` |
| password missing | **400** | 1200 | `UserName and Password required.` |
| username missing | **400** | 1200 | `UserName and Password required.` |
| both blank | **400** | 1200 | `UserName and Password required.` |

## Why the loop is outside `test()`

```ts
for (const testCase of cases.cases) {
  test(`${testCase.expectedStatus} — ${testCase.name}`, async ({ request }) => { ... });
}
```

| Loop position | Result |
|---|---|
| **Outside** `test()` | five separate tests; a failure names the case |
| Inside `test()` | one test that stops at the first failure |

Same rule as [week4/day4_2](/learn/w4/d4/p2). Putting the case name in the title is what
makes the report readable.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## The case that does not fit the table

"A duplicate username is refused" needs a username that already exists - a **prerequisite**, not
a data row. So it gets its own test.

Not everything belongs in the JSON, and forcing it there produces a table with a special-case
column that only one row uses.

And the result is worth remembering:

| Duplicate | Status | Code |
|---|---|---|
| **user** | **406** Not Acceptable | 1204 |
| **book** | **400** Bad Request | 1210 |

Same API, same kind of conflict, two different codes. Assert the family; probe the number.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| The loop inside `test()` | one test, and only the first failure is reported |
| A generic test title | the report says `case 3` and you go hunting |
| Expected values guessed, not probed | a lesson that fails on day one |
| The valid row not cleaned up | a new user on a shared API every run |
| Forcing a prerequisite case into the table | a column only one row uses |

**Next:** [Day 5.3 - The next step: fixtures](/learn/w7/d5/p3)

| | `beforeAll` + helper | fixture |
|---|---|---|
| Setup runs | once per describe | when a test asks |
| A test that needs no account | pays anyway | pays nothing |
| Teardown | a separate `afterAll` you must remember | next to the setup |
| If setup fails | a confusing hook error | the fixture is named in the failure |
| Shared across files | import the helper in each | import one `test` |

That is the same progression as week 5: page objects by hand
([week5/day3_2](/learn/w5/d3/p2)), then page objects as fixtures
([week5/day4_2](/learn/w5/d4/p2)). The pattern does not care whether it is holding a page or
an account.
Three fewer users created per run, on an API you do not own.

## What week 8 does with all this

You have the mechanics. Week 8 uses them on a different API (`restful-booker`) and pushes further:

| week8 | Adds |
|---|---|
| [day1_2](/learn/w8/d1/p2) | `request.newContext()`, PUT vs PATCH measured, token lifecycle |
| [day1_3](/learn/w8/d1/p3) | an API client as a fixture |
| [day2_2](/learn/w8/d2/p2) | negative scenarios where the **API is at fault**, `expect().rejects` |
| [day3_2](/learn/w8/d3/p2) | `$$eval` and scraping - back to the browser |

Seeing two real APIs is the point. `restful-booker` accepts a blank first name and returns 200
for wrong credentials; demoqa returns 406 for a duplicate user and 400 for a duplicate book.
Neither is *wrong* - which is why you probe rather than assume.

## API and UI in one test

The combination the session was building towards, and the reason a single tool for both matters:

```ts
test("a booking made by API appears in the UI", async ({ request, page }) => {
  const account = await createAccount(request);          // fast setup, no browser
  await page.goto("/login");                             // then check what a person sees
  ...
});
```

| Do this by | Because |
|---|---|
| API | setup, data creation, teardown - it is ~10x faster |
| UI | the one assertion that needs a human's view |

Asking for both `request` and `page` in one test is all it takes. No extra library, which was the
session's closing point about Playwright.

# Week 7, Day 5.4 - Practice

The last two close out the week.

## Week 7 done

| Day | You can now |
|---|---|
| 1 | say what TypeScript adds to JavaScript, and which tool catches a type error |
| 2 | read an API's docs, name the four status families, and never trust a code alone |
| 3 | write API tests with `request` instead of `page` |
| 4 | capture an id from one response and use it in the next, headers included |
| 5 | remove the duplication, drive negatives from data, and see where fixtures go next |

Every status code and message in these lessons was probed against the live API before it was
written down.

problems.statement:
**Add to the helper**
Add `addBook(request, account, isbn)` and `booksOf(request, account)` to a copy of
`api-helpers.ts`.

**Right when:** a spec adds a book and reads the collection back without writing a URL.

**Two more data rows**
Add a very long username and one with a space to the JSON table. Predict the status **before**
running.

**Right when:** you were right, or you were wrong and can say what the API does instead.

**The loop in the wrong place**
Move the `for` inside `test()`.

**Right when:** the report shows one test instead of five, and you can say which failures you
stopped being able to see.

**Build the fixture**
Write `api-fixtures.ts` from [day5_3](/learn/w7/d5/p3) and convert your Day 4 journey to it.

**Right when:** no `beforeAll` and no `afterAll` remain, and a deliberately failing test still
deletes its user.

**Prove the fixture is lazy**
Add a `console.log` inside it, then run a test that does not ask for `account`.

**Right when:** the line does not appear - and appears as soon as a test names the fixture.

**API setup, UI assertion**
Write one test that creates data through the API and checks something through the browser. Use
any UI app from an earlier week.

**Right when:** one test asks for both `request` and `page`, and you can say which part took
longer.

**Compare two APIs**
Send the same three malformed requests to demoqa and to `restful-booker` (week8's API).

**Right when:** you have a table of six responses and can name one place they disagree about what
a status code means.

**Audit your own suite**
Take every API spec you wrote this week and check it against the [day4_3](/learn/w7/d4/p3) reviewer's
checklist.

**Right when:** you have a count per row - and you fixed the "created and never deleted" ones
first.
